posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
It's time for the monthly progress report!
A lot of what I am going to cover today was actually covered in my last dev stream. Honestly, you'd probably get all the information faster by reading this, rather than watching it; but watching it might include some additional insights and thought processes behind my decision making if that is something that interests you.
The video is here:
FAST TRAVEL & FAST TRAVERSAL
First, I want to talk about my new fast travel system. I believe it was Mr.
@RCXGaming
who talked about the importance of fast travel systems in modern games. He helped motivate me to think about traversal, and after letting
@TESTOSTERONE
, Wind Ryder himself, get special access to an extremely busted build of the game, he pretty much set in stone the importance of reworking traversal in my game; mainly within the Cave level (the level that the beta test from last year took place in).
Spoiler:
Redoing fast travel event
So it's funny to me, that I clearly was aware how important quick traversal was in the first level I built, the Seas, because from its inception it had both a key item that could be used to create a short-cut and a teleportation system to jump around to specific points on the map.
However, I had tunnel vision (ha) on how I wanted my Cave to be formatted. I felt like these tools could not be used in the level. But thanks to RCX and Wind Ryder, I folded on this.
So in my efforts to improve traversal, firstly, I remastered my teleportation system so I could implement it into the Cave.
The new teleportation system looks like this:
This video was made mostly to show off some of the sound design work I had done (Including positional audio), but it also shows off how it works.
Basically; the player will unlock new fast travel points as they explore the level. Once unlocked, they can jump to it at any point in time - pretty standard fast travel system.
However, what you don't see in the video is the "Restore Fidel's Position" function.
RESTORE POINTS, QUICKLY GET BACK TO THE ACTION!
Spoiler:
Restore Fidel's Position
At its absolute basic functionality, it is just a checkpoint system. Whenever you change map or reach certain trigger zones, your position will be saved to a checkpoint.
In my game, whenever you die, you are brought back to town. This checkpoint system means that after you are done fiddling around in town, you can go to the teleporter and jump back to the last checkpoint before you died.
What is unique about this is functionality that had to be built into it because of the way players are able to play the game.
It's a nonlinear game, so players can take on any level they want at any time they want whenever they want. So it is very much possible for a player to go to one level (let's say the cave) and then die (or save and quit - we'll talk about this later), and then decide that they'd rather make some progress in a different level (let's say the Seas.)
With a typical checkpoint system, you are just constantly overwriting your checkpoint with the most recent checkpoint. Well if that's how I did it, then if the player decided to go to the Seas, then when they return to the Cave and use "Restore Fidel's Position", Fidel would be brought back to the Seas. Oh dear. Now poor Fidel would have to trek all the way back to where she left off in her Cave Adventure because she dared to take a break and adventure around the Seas.
So, the checkpoints are unique to each level. When you select "Restore Fidel's Position", Fidel will be restored back to the most recent check point within that specific level!
That pretty much covers the fast travel system so far. So in a nutshell,
Players can unlock dedicated fast travel points as they explore and use those points to quickly jump to different portions of the level.
Players have checkpoints independent to each level of the game, and when returning to the level, they can use the fast travel system to jump back to their most recent checkpoint.
Next is traversing specifically the Cave...
REVOLUTIONARY DESIGN: GOING UP
AND
DOWN
Spoiler:
One-way design is gone.
The cave was designed with this idea of "one way forward." The fish mechanic - allowing the player to catch a fish then throw said fish into lava to create a temporary platform across (yes it's silly) - is designed to facilitate the one way direction of the cave. Once you jump across your temporary fish platform, there may not be a fish to catch on the other side to go back.
The cave being split into what I called a "right ribbon" and "left ribbon" (called ribbons because it's a thin, long, linear path that loops back around on itself), the right ribbon puzzle gimmick is that the player could only test the results of their puzzling later. With the actual elements that control aspects of the puzzle on the lower part of the ribbon, and the ability to complete the puzzle on the upper part of the ribbon, the player needed to observe carefully what the puzzle elements are doing, and have the foresight for how those puzzle elements should be set up for the future.
If the puzzle elements were not set up properly: bad news: It's a one way trip back down the cliff face for you to adjust the puzzle elements, then have to shamefully walk all the way back around to the upper ribbon again. (And sometimes that could be a really long walk).
This is really unfairly punishing to the player. So to alleviate this unnecessary back-tracking, I have changed all of the one-way jump-down points to points where the player can place a ladder to climb down or up.
While both of these updates break the original philosophy of the Caves design, I feel like these improvements both improve the overall experience (making it less stressful) and better aligns with the overall philosophy of the entire game which is to play however you want.
Next up is Parallaxing! Let's make those maps beautiful!
MAKING MAGNIFICENT MAPS
I have been struggling with the flat look of my game. It's hard to put into words other than "flat" to describe my game, but it's just this feeling that things aren't really popping out. I talked about this in my previous update post on the game, so we'll just gloss over this. (You can read more about it in this post here:
LINK TO POST #
)
I started by doing a few tests on the on-going Forest level, then decided to test to see if this could be applied to The Seas level (which has the largest map in the game). As mentioned, this was talked about in the previous update, so let's move on:
Spoiler:
The Results (featuring images!)
Now I have finished all of the maps for the Forest level, and all of those initial experiments helped me find some techniques that both speed up the process while also adding more detailing work to the maps. There are 9 maps in total (for the Forest level), I won't share all of them, but take a look at a few of my favorites:
This is first map of the Forest. There is only faint shading, light ambient occlusion around corners plus a shadow on the factory in the top left, and "deep" and "shallow" waters in the Red Juice river. I plan to make a quick revision to this map using some of the newer techniques I used in the following maps...
The forest is designed as a 3x3 square, with each row being tiered above the other. Row 1 being the "highest point" in the forest, the lighting is gentler. Row 2 has slightly heavier shadows. Pictured above is from row 2. As you can see there is some stronger contrast and processing to add additional details to the map.
Row 3, as you can see is much darker, hopefully creating a feeling like you are in the "thick of the forest". One of the map overlays I used to add faux detailing is much more apparent here due to the added contrast between light and shadows.
Looking Ahead
Red Juice & The Fox
Currently I am working on improving the logic on a few aspects of the Forest. It's better to do it now than to have to do it later after all of the events have been placed. This is also mostly coming in the way of how to handle certain aspects (such as all the Red Juice resources) after the level is complete. Do I want the player to still gather those resources? Thematically it wouldn't make sense (your goal is to cure the forest of it's Red Juice ailment), but it would serve a game play purpose.
The item you unlock in the Forest (as previously discussed in this update:
LINK TO POST #
) allows Fidel to change into a fox:
However, this form requires Red Juice. After the forest is complete, the readily available Red Juice resource would be depleted, obviously making it tough to stay in the fox form if you can't get the resources to sustain it.
On the one hand, I considered adding a quest that would allow you to permanently switch between Fidel and the Fox without the requirement of resources, but that is additional scope. Maybe in the future this can be added.
In the mean time, I decided that one Red Vine tree will get planted in the town center (bye-bye fountain!) after the player completes the Forest level. Therefore, the player will be able to interact with this tree at any time and extract some Red Juice for the adventure ahead.
Load game, Return Home
This is still something that is in the
"I'm thinking…"
stage, but I am thinking of changing how the whole save system works in my game.
Spoiler:
Anti-save scum, philosophy matching save & load!
I have already partially achieved this by creating a call-able autosave event that will overwrite your existing save. This is to prevent save scumming by just aggressively and constantly overwriting your existing save to prevent you from "rewinding time".
However, the new part of this is how to handle loading the game there after.
I am thinking that whenever the player loads their game, they will be returned to the town. Easy enough to execute at it's most basic form; I already have a plugin to run a on-game-load common event. However, there are many situations where I DON'T want the player to be returned to town otherwise it might break things.
The pros:
It encourages one of the main pillars of my game: interacting with the town. It's just another way to encourage players to not ignore it if the game is constantly gravitating Fidel back to town.
It hopefully encourages players to consider their quit points; both discouraging quitting mid-level, while encouraging quitting when back in town ("Well, I'm already in town, so might as well quit now.")
The Cons:
Both of those pros can also be cons, being brought back to town means the tedious trek back to where you left off.
It will probably take a lot of tedious work searching and accounting for the edge cases where I would want to disable the on-game-load common event. Missing even 1 spot where the common event should be disabled could potentially result in soft-locks and completely destroying a save file.
As of now this has not been implemented (if that wasn't obvious already), however I will continue to think about it.
Fidel & The Maker's Trial
(The OG, the prototype)
​
At
@TRIDIUM
's request, and because
@hiddenone
is kind enough to play my jank old game, I'm going to link it here and make this more obviously public. This is the prototype to Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox and was a game I developed in a month just to help me come to grips with RPG Maker.
Fidel & The Maker's Trial by NolanAlighieri
Fidel is faced with the challenges of learning game design, but The Maker intends to stop her.
nolanalighieri.itch.io
To be absolutely clear: This game has nothing to do with the current Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox project other than in name.
Spoiler:
It's pretty jank, here's some info about it...
It's about 2 hours long (depending on your RPG-ing/Puzzling abilities) and I think has some cool ideas that were obviously not well executed. Some of the foundation of
Pauper's Paradox
is there, but I can promise you that
Pauper's Paradox
has refined...uh...most everything you see in this OG prototype. Those who play
Maker's Trial
now are likely playing the best version of it due to the number of updates I have done since it's launch. I still support the game, if not a bit irregularly.
It is filled with some jank, I don't intend on fixing it, however I do still enjoy the project for what it is, so if there are major errors such as critical bugs (such as softlocks or crashes), balancing problems, or minor grammatical issues then I can issue an update. (I might only issue an update for grammatical issues if there are other issues to fix too. No reason to push a full update for a typo)
Any feedback you do provide, however, will help me consider design choices for Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox or future projects, so while I don't intend on changing much of the OG, the feedback will still be valuable.
If you leave feedback on the OG game, it would be appreciated if you title your post or include bold text to indicate that it is feedback for the prototype/OG. This will reduce possible confusion as to which game is getting feedback
And that's it for this month's update! Thank you everyone for your continued support and interest in Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox's development!

Beyond being a wannabe game dev, there wasn't much to her character that stood out to make me connect with her and I think that was mostly because she was only responding to the negative comments. There were a number of ways her personality could have been fleshed out (having her comment on things more, give herself little pep talks, small celebrations when completing a puzzle, etc.), though I can understand not focusing on that and instead focusing on the gameplay.
Not gonna touch mapping, you know the quality level that was there.
Using save crystals is a nice idea, but that does mean that players who may need to quit to take care of something (pets, kids, late for work) could lose a good chunk of their progress. And for this short game it wouldn't really be worth redoing a lot of the puzzles, so you could lose players who would have otherwise finished the game. Striking a balance with an emergency save item that doesn't heal and can only be used once before needing to be restored at a save crystal would give players that safety net to quit and run off without having to worry about their progress.
Puzzles were a big part of the game, and unfortunately I think a lot of them suffered from "new dev-itis". Boulder pushing and jumping puzzles can be fun, but the quirks in them really showed that you weren't familiar with eventing or planning them in RM. The ways boulders could be moved didn't have much rhyme or reason to me as a player, sometimes they could roll only one direction and sometimes they couldn't. Pushing puzzles can be a great way to challenge players but you want to keep the rules consistent, so having marks either on the floor or on the boulder to show which directions they can roll would be good. If you wanted to do away with boulders completely, creating tracks in the floors and stylized puzzle pieces could be an interesting replacement.
There was a silly bug with the first boulder you interact with, I tried to push it from the side before the fight but couldn't, so once I won and was able to move the boulder I pushed up upwards and blocked myself. So of course I chose to reset it... Which ended up with me moved back to the start and the boulder vanishing completely from the map. I could keep going, so it was fine, but seemed like an odd thing to happen.
I also ran into a bug with the boulders new the first crystal, where the far right boulder didn't move and instead a fourth boulder appeared. If that wasn't a bug and was meant to happen, then some dialogue would've been good to clue me in to that not being a dev mistake and instead how the game would mess with me as a player.
The jump puzzles were okay, but I think having the player need to hit a button every time to jump was overkill. A lot of the later jump 'puzzles' were just paths, long ones at that, so it was me just holding a direction and spamming spacebar to reach the next puzzle section. Perhaps having it start with a button and then being able to jump just by touching the jump events would be nicer, your players should be able to figure that out and then can focus on the puzzle itself and not having to click all the time.
Next up, let's talk about the battles. For the most part I did actually enjoy the fights, the limited enemies and weaknesses meant that I learned what skills to use on each enemy quickly and they were quick enough (for the most part) that the battle screen didn't overstay its welcome. Gaining MP from being hit does make for an interesting mechanic, and it was nice to not have to save my MP or potions for emergency battles like in some games. The miniboss battles that blocked levers were different enough to make me think a bit and not just spam the attack button.
Though it did take me a while to figure out why there was a timer after every battle, it would have been good to explain that quickly after the first fight.
The Maker battle and the Worse Thought battle are where the battle system really falls apart. Both were much longer than they really needed to be, and instead of making me feel dread or depressed they just annoyed me. That may be because I deal with negative thoughts by imagining them coming from a little bothersome gremlin, so when the Maker and Thoughts were being negative I was just going "yeah yeah, back to your cave you little green ball of negativity". The Maker battle felt like the final battle, so dealing with the Worse Thought battle after that didn't add much to my experience. The fact that I was meant to lose that battle was disappointing, while I do get the point story-wise, it wasn't clear since I could do damage and I was able to defeat Bad Thoughts. Once I realized that Worse Thought was able to heal itself fully and that I needed to kill Fidel to end the game, it meant I had to still run through a bunch more turns because I had been healing with items. Sneaking in a 'Give Up' skill after a few turns of Worse Thoughts buffeting Fidel would have gotten the same results (most players would keep trying for a little while before using that skill) without having to take so many extra turns.
You can also open the menu after losing the Worse Thought fight and as the camera pans away from the fainted Fidel, which does take away from the scene. I assume the cutscene was done with a parallel process instead of autorun, but that should be easy to fix.
Overall, as you mentioned before it's definitely a janky game. But if you've taken the good points from this game and polished those, then I'm looking forward to playing Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox and seeing just how much you've improved.

It's definitely hard to find the right balance, especially when it comes to puzzles since players think about things so differently. For your old game, it's probably fine to leave as-is if you haven't touched it already and just know that some players will get tired of it.
For jump puzzles pushing a button doesn't make me feel like I'm really contributing to solving the puzzle (though mostly because I have creaky joints so when I hit spacebar my knuckles often pop and distract me), but having to pause and think about which jump will take me to the right spot and which will lead me to a dead end will make me totally focus on the game's world. It's a different design philosophy, but personally I think when it comes to puzzle-heavy games it's better to "automate" a lot of the mechanics so the player can focus on solving the puzzles and not which button to push at that moment; instead of pushing a button to jump it's automatic when the player tries to walk towards the space, interacting with a lever will reset a pushing puzzle without giving a 'yes/no' prompt since if the player is clicking on it they likely want it to activate, etc.
It does depend on the gameplay you want to create though, so I get it if taking away too much of those player interactions with the game go against what you're aiming to make.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
Whoops, looks like I missed my December update. I was pretty busy between the November update to when I would normally do the December update so not as much got done on the game during that time, so I didn't have much to report anyways.
Let's jump right in! It's a big one with lots of pictures and gifs!
Gift Giving In Action
​
I finally got around to implementing my gift-giving system into the game. It has existed for a long time as basically just a database object with no actual interaction in game. That has changed.
The gift giving system was created to answer a major problem with my game; the lack of rewards for going off the beaten path.
(It's a good read, even though it's long. There's some pretty pictures to look at)
Spoiler:
The Theory Behind It
After watching SG Harlekin stream my old beta, one of the complaints he had was that the maps were big, not necessarily empty. He seemed to praise the mapping, but lacking stuff to do.
Here's the challenge:
How do I reward the player for going off the beaten path?
The obvious answer is "A chest, you dummy!"
But sometimes the "off the beaten path" way isn't really far enough out of the way or challenging enough to warrant a chest. So what do you do then?
I believe this is a common problem all JRPGs tend to encounter whenever they try to do wider, more open maps, and they have had a solution to this problem for it for quite a few generations of gaming.
pictured above: Blue Reflection: Tie, Ao picking up a crafting material item drop.
Crafting materials.
Crafting materials are
a
reward for going off the beaten path, but are minor enough that you aren't overly-rewarding the player for something menial.
The problem is that crafting can create a whole new scope of items and balancing that need to be accounted for. It can be quite complicated to implement in more facets than one. In the scope of my game, crafting just wasn't the answer.
Unlikely Inspiration:
But probably not surprising considering how often I have referenced this game as an unlikely inspiration for Fidel.
In Heroes of Might and Magic, you can find treasure boxes in your exploration. The fascinating thing with these treasure boxes is that they aren't like other resources. Resources you find just lying around on the play field are just picked up like a typical resource. Treasure boxes present a simple, but interesting choice:
Never say I don't put effort into these posts. I re-installed Heroes 4 just to capture this gif.
When you touch the treasure box, you are asked whether you want to take the gold for yourself, or to donate it (that's the role-play reason) to receive a bounty of experience points for your hero.
I've actually really like this system. The challenge is that I cannot copy this system 1-to-1 in my game, because in a sense, EXP plays more of a neutral role in the game. If you've read previous updates, I effectively removed leveling from my game. You still "level up" (now called ranking up) because this helps dictate gold drops, player luck, and enemy difficulty. Due to enemies becoming more difficult at higher ranks, some players may wish to stay at a certain rank, thus negating the desire for more EXP.
However, the idea I had initially settled upon was that the player can give the presents to any of the NPCs they want. There is no affinity or romance system, but instead certain NPCs would "thank the player" for the gift by giving them 1 of 3 different rewards assigned to that specific NPC:
Community Experience (leveling up the town)
Player Experience (ranking up the player)
Notes (money)
Each category would only be a small pittance, but the player could decide to just give many gifts to a single NPC get get a lot of rewards for their kindness.
I did ultimately decide to step back a little bit from this idea. Giving a gift will always grant a tiny amount of Community EXP. Undecided, but I may have NPC's give 1 of 2 awards assigned to that NPC: Either notes or
Gratitude tokens
.
But...
Gratitude Tokens
? What's that?
And notes...hmmm, that sort of contrasts with...
AAA Was Right! Loot Boxes are a Great Idea!
​
So it seemed like an obvious answer to just let the player character open the present item they found on the map and receive a random reward like a loot box. I already thought of that when I first conceived the idea of the gift system. To explain why I was opposed to implementing that before ultimately changing my mind, we need a little more context.
Spoiler:
Context for No Loot Boxes
Initially I didn't want to provide this option to the player because the point was to encourage further interaction with the town, as well as an underlying theme in the game which is kindness. So I didn't want to allow the player to just open the presents selfishly for themselves when ultimately I want them to interact with the town and also to help emphasize the themes of kindness.
I felt like no matter what I needed to encourage players by offering some sort of reward, otherwise the system would just feel pointless. I just have to get over the fact that natural kindness cannot be encouraged, it just has to be exhibited normally. So there needed to be an "ultimate goal" for giving the presents.
See, with the introduction of ranks in my game, experience was no longer a good reward for the player. Community EXP is worthwhile, but will eventually be useless, and is pretty easy to earn, so it's not super worthwhile to get community EXP. So last is money - notes. That remains valuable in the game at least, but then it just feels like the player is giving the gifts to NPCs for selfish reasons, which is sort of counter to the theme I wanted.
This is where the
Gratitude Tokens
come in to play. I will come back to this, but let's first talk about these loot boxes.
So, the "loot-boxes" actually don't reward the player much at all. After all, the loot boxes (presents) are pretty commonly found throughout the world. So if they had good rewards in them, they would over shadow chests in the game, which are supposed to be the main provider of good rewards.
So there is a very, very high chance that the player will receive just 3 notes from opening the present
(which isn't much in my game's economy - about a 1/5 of the way to a low-level healing item - or about 1 Mac on the
Big Mac Index
.)
Then there is a small chance the player might earn some sort of consumable.
Finally, there is some logic that tracks how the player is doing in the game. If the player (according to the logic) seems to be having a hard time, the odds begin to tilt in favor of the consumables, with a small chance of getting a "treasure bag", which contains a handful of notes and 1 of each type of consumable. But the treasure bag cannot be received until the player has first crossed a specified threshold of "having trouble".
Give A Man A Fish...
​
So what are these
Gratitude Tokens
?
Gratitude Tokens
are given to the player by the NPCs of the town as a thanks for the player's kindness.
There is a mysterious hidden chamber housing the hooked fish of Gratitude.
This fish will reward the player's kindness to the towns folk.
The text seen in the gif is obviously just placeholder.
When the player speaks to the Fish of Gratitude, the player will be given a choice of 3 different options.
Permanently increase the player's STACK RATE stat (basically luck)
Permanently increase the effectiveness of the healing skill.
Permanently increase the starting ConP when entering combat.
Spoiler:
Infinite Power
This is actually a form of indefinite power gain, if the player so chose to grind it out, but each time you accept a reward from the Gratitude Fish, the cost of
Gratitude Tokens
increases 2 fold. (I do plan to put a cap on it, first to prevent rare cases of over-flow - not sure how the engine handles overflow, but not gonna mess with it and just cap it. Additionally, if I just let it infinitely double the amount of tokens required it would reach an impossibly high number. I want to cap it at a "very high" number, but still with in the realm of possibility to grind out for)
Choosing these 3 stats was actually quite difficult. As mentioned in the OP of this thread, Fidel really strips back a lot of the JRPG complexity, which means I have less stats and numbers to play around with, meaning less parameters to boost as rewards or items to give.
These 3 stats seemed the most balanced stats to allow for infinite growth of.
Stack rate may potentially be the most powerful of the 3, but there are plenty of other ways of boosting stack rate late game. This just allows the player more flexibility in their build if by gaining that additional stack rate from somewhere else.
Healing is of course pretty important, but also at it's base is pretty powerful; since this is a single actor game, healing naturally provides a turn of increased damage reduction so that player's don't get caught in a healing cycle. I'd say boosting this stat effectively just acts as quality of life.
Battle's start at reduced ConP (the starting ConP value is based on the player's rank), so the starting ConP basically acts as a "head start" when entering combat, but is by no means necessary, as ConP can pretty quickly be gained in combat by just guarding and tanking a few hits. And again, late game items and builds can off-set how long it takes to build up ConP.
As you might be able to tell, the gift giving system has quite a lot of complexity to it:
First there is retrieving the gift, probably the easiest part.
Then the decision the player can make: Open the gift now or give it to an NPC?
If the player opens it, there is the loot box mechanic and the logic to determine the reward.
If the player gifts it to the NPC, the NPC needs to react appropriately (something I didn't even talk about in this post) and reward the player with a gratitude token.
The player can then take the gratitude token to receive a permanent upgrade from the Gratitude Fish.
So this is how I have spent a lot of my time developing the game these past months. However, there are a few more things I would like to talk about if you would bare with me.
A New Team Member
​
If you looked carefully at those Gifs I posted, you might have been thinking, "Hmm, the player character doesn't really look like Fidel...."
That is correct!
As usual, a story...
Spoiler:
Fidel Got Tall
For a long time now, I have - at the very least - wanted to replace the stupid looking bean-faced SV battler for Fidel. I've never been happy with how it looks. The expression on the actor doesn't fit Fidel, and I am not a fan of the style the RTP uses for battlers.
@TESTOSTERONE
had played a jank version of my game and even commented that replacing the battlers would go a long way for the feel of the game. While he wasn't necessarily referencing the walk sprites of the world, I had this feeling that maybe tall overworld sprites would also change the feeling of the game.
As a test, I decided to plop one of the premade templates
@WTR
had made,
seen in this thread
. Immediately I could feel how the game changed. It's like this one small change was entirely new coat of paint. From that point, I began investigating what it might cost to do tall sprites for my game. I knew that I would need all sprites to be in the exact same style, otherwise things would obviously look out of place. So if I have 1 custom sprite made for my game, then all NPCs would need to be custom.
I did reach out to WTR about commissioning them. However, they very politely declined; understandably - and I am thankful they even responded to me at all. So, if you see this WTR: thanks once again for taking the time to reply to me!
My search eventually lead me to an artist known as
TheJuneBug
on Pixiv. TheJuneBug has experience working with game engines; primarily Unity, but also some RPG Maker experience as well. TheJuneBug is hoping to one day create his own RPG in MZ/MV but definitely not Unite.
Although he permits reposting his work, I'd rather you just go to his profile and check his stuff.
(I assume she's a she)
He's a he, my bad.
He will be doing the pixel art for my characters in the game! His first work has been delivered and I am very happy with the results.
This is Trisha, one of the towns folk, with a solemn back story that Fidel will need to find a way to console her grief.
But in the mean time, this is the form Fidel is taking while I wait for more great art to be done by TheJuneBug!
Finally,
The Old Game Got Updated (finally)
​
@hiddenone
was so kind to play my old janky game. I promised an update would come from her feedback, and that sat on the back burner for a long time until finally during my winter holiday I cracked open my old project and made some changes.
Here are the highlights:
The final boss had it's HP reduced by 20%. Still probably not enough, but oh well
The new "Give Up" skill was added. This is just a "kill-self" skill, which might be useful for speeding up a certain fight
Save Crystal added! This allows the player to save the game ONCE at any time, any place.
Rogue boulder was fixed by completely redoing the logic.
Jump logic was adjusted slightly. After activating the first jump, Fidel will continue to jump the same direction. Only whenever the player needs to change direction will the player need to activate the jump again.
If you didn't play the old, janky game, you can find it here:
Fidel & The Mater's Trial
(I typoed Maker as Mater, but I am keeping it)
I know I'm not selling you too hard on it by calling it jank, but once you get past the jank, I do think there is something to enjoy about it.

Hello everyone!
It’s another month. This month’s update is coming a little bit later than usual because I was waiting for June to complete some art.
But more on that in a minute!
First I would like to talk about the game progress itself.
I wanted to shift focus from the Forest level back to the town. The primary reason is that I hope to do another round of closed
beta
alpha testing soon. In the alpha test, it is unlikely the forest would be accessible. If I were to make the forest level accessible, it would likely require a much longer period of development time to ensure it’s at least ready for testing.
So with that being said...
let’s see what January and the first half of February brought with it!
Spoiler:
Everette
Everette, a resolute mother who  prioritizes her child's future over their own immediate welfare, and has grown increasingly exasperated by her husband's laissez-faire parenting, fostering a schism within the family unit.
Unlike other townsfolk in Crossroad Commune, Everette is not intended to have a vignette (a short story covering a theme, idea, or topic). This is primarily due to scope. As I was writing out her dialogue, I saw how there could be a vignette around her ideals and how she might grow as a person, but I’ll have to save that for another time (maybe an update post launch if this game finds any modicum of success?).
However, rather than give her nothing, she does have some unique interactions:
June is hard at work preparing Everette’s sprite now. In the meantime enjoy the drafts you see here, and don’t mind the char-gen used in GIF.
As the player progresses, talks to her and her family more, and gives gifts (
see my previous update
), she will begin to warm up to Fidel and become softer over time.
How this is performed is actually a bit more complicated than you might expect, as she runs a calculation every time you talk to her which will check the aforementioned items to determine what stage she is at (of 4 stages of happiness), then a random variable will pick 1 of 3 possible responses she can give the player within that stage. So beyond her introduction, this gives her a possibility of 12 responses.
The hope is that she will rarely give the same response to the player twice (It’s also worth noting you cannot talk to her twice in a row. You must leave the house and re-enter if you want to talk to her again.)
There is also a hidden scene that shows a different side to her, but unlocking that scene requires very special conditions to be met. Don’t worry folks, if you miss it, you aren’t missing a core part of the story. It’s just a nice little bonus for others to discover.
Spoiler:
Quil
Quil, an angsty teenager consumed by love, and callously disregards those he holds dear.
His vignette delves into the departure of friendships, illustrating how diverging paths in adulthood often lead to either an abrupt farewell or a silent recollection between the people in our lives.
Quil’s story makes up a much larger story that also involves Trisha and Sena - who will be introduced in the future.
Taking a page out of my own level design book, I wanted to start fusing other genre types into the way these vignettes play out. This, first of all makes the cutscenes themselves far more interesting that 2 pixel blobs shouting text boxes at each other, but second it also helps make the execution (the “quest design”) of the vignettes more mechanically interesting as well.
I’ll discuss this “imaginative” form of the vignettes more in the future as they move from the script and into the game, but as an overview, there are planned genre blending with:
A detective/mystery genre
A walking-sim influenced “piece the story together” type section
A typical RPG horror game trope.
Until then, I composed a song that is relevant to one of those parts. Please take a listen.
This song was discussed in more depth over in the
sound design clinic thread
. There is some really neat stuff going on in this song, so I recommend reading it if you are into music stuff.
And finally, the moment you have all been waiting for…I think? Maybe.
Spoiler:
Movement & Action
There have been 2 major improvements to my game’s overall polish.
ACTION
Thanks to the help of
@SGHarlekin
, I’ve implemented some action sequencing. More will come in the future, but this was really more of a demo to see how it improved the feeling of combat.
In addition to all the fancy screen effects that the combat now features, the combat also moves much faster thanks to action sequencing.
This has greatly improved how combat feels.
MOVEMENT
You may have noticed those strange pink squares in previous gifs.
This is because I have implemented Chaucer’s
Collision Altering Plugin
. For dev purposes, the debug mode that shows collision data on tiles has been left on.
I was iffy about implementing pixel movement into my game. Fidel has mostly been designed with tile-based movement in mind.
In the past, I also played with other pseudo-pixel movement systems to see how it changes the feel, and while I liked it, it broke far too many things in my project to use.
However, I’ve been working really closely with Chaucer on this. He is one of the most active and supportive developers in the community. So getting things fixed, and getting things fixed fast is a huge factor as to why I will likely stick with this plugin.
It’s also hard to ignore how huge of a difference this makes to the overall feeling of the game. I enjoy that it feels like the player has a much more nuanced control over their character.
Most of the logic will continue to operate on a grid, and collision data will also likely be imprecise, but the results could not be ignored.
And that’s it for this month’s update!
It was a lot to cover as usual!
Don’t expect the fun title banners for every update here after. Just something fun I wanted to throw together for this update.
I hope this was an enjoyable read!

nolanalighieri.itch.io

DOWNLOAD
Now I will ramble about the new difficulty.
Why is Sport Difficulty tied to the Score Attack? And why Score Attack at all in an RPG game?
Spoiler:
The answer might shock you!
While I was watching Rebekah play my game, I realized that even on the default difficulty you can get through much of the first area with just your basic attack. It's not optimal at all, and battles will be a slog if you do so, but it is possible.
I realized I wanted to add a difficulty mode into the game that better reflected the OG difficulty which was quite demanding of players.
The problem is that so many of the balancing changes (especially the newly added limiter applied to enemy damage scaling) means it's virtually impossible to make the old difficulty a selectable difficulty without effectively doubling the database to have "current enemies and skills" and "1.0 enemies and skills". I mean, technically I could do that, but I don't want to put that much effort into updating this old jank game.
Leveling in the current form of the game makes the game become very easy in the latter half. So the answer was to limit leveling...by removing it.
But now that creates a new problem. If the player can't level at all, and there are no resources or gold in the game, what is the point of combat at all? Just run from every fight.
Okay, so to fix that I will disable running from encounters in this difficulty mode.
Well, now encounters just feel like a nuisance; just a road block/time waster.
Okay, let's score the player based on their performance!
And so the Sport Difficulty was born.
But, with the implementation of a score system, it felt silly to only tie it to the hardest difficulty. Maybe players want to go for a high score on other difficulties.
Thus, I separated out the score attack from the sport difficulty.
Let me tell you, getting my own personal high score to set as a default value in the game was a pain in the rear. But it did feel like quite the accomplishment to get my 7071 on sport mode with permadeath enabled! No items!
After my dev run to set the high score, I did actually change some of the score values, so it may, theoretically, be easier to reach that score.

Joy

​
Joy Hayward is a young girl, about the same age as Fidel, and knows that her delight causes the least disruption within the community. She is the daughter of Everette Hayward, the wife of Felix Hayward - the shop keeper of the town.
Although Felix is permissive and just wishes for Joy’s happiness in the present; Everett prioritizes Joy’s long-term success and happiness, finding that Fidel is just an annoying distraction from Joy’s studies.
Ever since the big bad Maker sealed off Crossroad Commune from the rest of the world, she’s been looking for a friend or a purpose. Fidel seemed to appear just at the right time.
BEYOND THE TOWN...
​
In Fidel & The Pauper’s Paradox
(or Fat PP)
, Fidel will be able to explore 3 different dungeons
(though only 2 are available in the beta test)
each with a new gadget to help expand her exploration capabilities.
Each dungeon is designed around different game genre ideas, making each dungeon unique in its structure.
ITEM FUSING
​
Finally, how about looking ahead into the future?
While play testing I discovered that the economy becomes broken quickly.
As a new player you'll probably find yourself strapped for cash frequently. However, the economy will eventually plateau once you buy all the gear you need. From that point forward the economy will balloon rather rapidly as the player has nothing to spend their hard earned coin on.
This came from the fact that once you buy the gear necessary for your build, there is no reason to save up for any other gear piece.
Likewise, since switching to the RANK system, there have been very little incentive to play at higher ranks.
(which I was going to link here, but I guess I never made a post about it!?! So I guess the length of this post is being doubled...)
So what I am considering is creating some sort of gear-fusing system, where you can fuse the attributes of a matching piece of gear into another piece for an increasingly higher and higher cost. This gives players a reason to buy all the other gear even when they don't need it, and it will allow the power scaling to go much higher, which means I can make the higher ranks more lethal BUT also reward players more adequately for taking on the challenge.
RANKING UP
replacing leveling up
​
Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox ran into a major problem.
See, the game is non-linear. This makes accounting for a difficulty curve quite challenging.
I knew this from the beginning and therefore had implemented scaling enemies. However, when Diablo 4 launched and the discussion around scaling enemies ramped up, I decided to rethink how I handled levels and enemies...
Spoiler:
RANK explanation
The conclusion I came to was what I call the RANK system.
Earning new ranks is not much different than a regular leveling system - kill things, get exp. But unlike leveling, ranking up
DOES NOT
increase your stats.
However, ranking up does increase the enemy difficulty. This does not necessarily mean just giving a stat boost to enemies (though sometimes it does). It also includes enemies unlocking new skills, having more aggressive AI, among other things to ramp up the challenge.
The system is constantly trying to push you, the player, into taking on harder and harder challenges. However, at the very core of Fidel & The Pauper's Paradox is the ability to play how you want.
By going to Truette, the town priest, the player is able to set their rank to any previously unlocked rank.
For a small donation the player can RANK down if they want to reduce the difficulty, or for an even smaller donation, the player rank RANK up to return to the highest rank they previously achieved. (See, constantly trying to push you towards harder challenges.)
Oh, but what if a player gets locked into a challenge soft-lock; too high of a rank to defeat the enemies, but too broke to lower their rank?
Well, being defeated in combat will lower your RP (rank points - basically exp). If you are defeated enough times, you will rank down.

Heyas, I got to play the beta version and now y'all get to suffer through another one of my essays.
I had fun, but it really needs some more balancing when it comes to battles to make it enjoyable in the full game.
Spoiler:
Feedback
I'll start with some of the stuff I loved. The maps are lovely, Fidel is adorable in both her art and her characterization, and while there wasn't a lot of plot revealed while I was playing the bits that I saw were intriguing. I did enjoy exploring the areas, though Fidel's walk speed is painfully slow so being able to move faster would have improved that a bunch. Each NPC felt distinct, and I was looking forward to getting to know them more (though they didn't seem to have anything else to say after their introduction cutscenes).
That said, this is very clearly still early in development. The concepts are there and there are glimmers of a great game, but it needs a lot more tweaking and polishing to really make for a fun game to play. The cutscenes are interesting, but they are quite long. Especially in the start of the game, it feels like it will focus on character interactions before all that gets tossed aside to go explore dungeons and face off against monsters. I think the two parts need to be better connected in the start to make it all more cohesive, maybe a weak enemy troop enters into town right before the player gets control so Fidel has to fight and the NPCs can comment on Fidel being able to help out their situation (or comment on how a little girl shouldn't have to deal with the adults' problems). That would help make it feel like Fidel beating the dungeons is focusing on helping solve the town's problems instead of how it currently feels like Fidel just wanders around and happens to help.
Battles are where this game really suffers, and it unfortunately drags the whole experience down. Even the intro battle with the Maker dragged on for way too long, and while it was nice to get to play around with all my skills I wish the Maker had talked during the battle so that I knew it wasn't one I was ever meant to win. Once I finished exploring the town I started out in the Seas area, and the battles felt unbalanced instantly. I mostly fought troops with three or four enemies, and each enemy needed at least four attacks to be killed. Add in the fact I needed to gain ConP to do real damage, and it felt like I was spending 5+ minutes in each mob fight... All to be rewarded with a handful of Notes, which weren't enough to buy any new weapons or accessories. I kept doing every battle I saw because I wanted to try out another weapon, but by the time I finally gathered enough I had defeated the fish boss and didn't really have a reason to stay in the Seas area except for exploration.
The fact that I lost a lot of the skills I had during the Maker fight also hurt. I had enjoyed using Double Stack (even though it has some problems), and being limited to only one move per turn just made each battle drag on and on. If there were less enemies in each fight or if I kept the ability to attack twice a turn it would have made combat a lot swifter and more enjoyable.
The magic attacks also suffered heavily in battle, and I ended up pretty much only using Butane Lighter since it cost 5 ConP compared to the others' 6, and had the chance to do 1 HP damage each turn. The magic skills were supposed to be a big part of combat since you could stack and do more damage depending on what state the enemy had, but the actual probability of inflicting a state was so low that I rarely saw it more than once a battle. Since I couldn't consistently inflict a state, I just used the skill that cost the least amount of ConP and did more damage than the default Attack. Speaking of ConP, it was also a pain that Fidel didn't start with any. I can understand not giving the player a full bar at the start of a battle, but a random amount between 4-7 would jumpstart the whole battle and give the player more choices from the start instead of having to wait a few turns to use a skill.
In battle I found myself rarely using items, except for the boss fight, because enemies did so little damage that I could safely use Poise for a few turns in a row to gain enough ConP to heal. The idea behind the items and having items found in Presents that could be instead given to NPCs is neat, but since I so rarely went back into town due to not having many Notes I found myself opening all the Presents for some instant goodies. While I know you plan on adding more to the gift-giving system, the game's current state just doesn't make it feel worthwhile.
I do want to touch on the meta bits of the game, since there's something cool there. The intro starts the player in a very 'gamedev test room' type place, so I was looking forward to seeing more of that scattered around the game to hint at even more secrets and story beats. But for the most part I didn't get to see anything else fun. The teleportation pads invoked the same sterile white of the intro and the touch with opening a menu to click 'transfer' is great and got my mind overanalyzing what it could all mean. But for the most part that was the only place the meta parts would pop back up, and it would have been way more interesting to see it in NPC cutscenes (such as having a choice when responding where one option is clearly terrible, and the cutscene 'restarts' if it's chosen) and in battles (maybe one skill could scramble the enemy and makes it an error instead of a normal confusion state). If you want there to be a meta story beyond the main story, then you really need to weave it through more of the gameplay and maps. If you just want a few points where it's a nod to other devs or just to look cool, then I'd consider cutting it out entirely and focusing on Fidel's story in the world.
All that said, I do want to make sure it's clear that I enjoyed the concept behind this game and want to play more! It's just that the main points of gameplay need more work and sour the whole thing at the moment.
tldr, here are the "things that must be fixed" highlights:
Cutscenes need tightened up, characterization is good but they just take too long
Movement speed needs upped
Battles need to lose a few enemies per troop, lower the HP of everyone, start Fidel with some ConP, and give more Notes as a reward
If you want to lean into the meta effects, then really go for it. Otherwise ditch it entirely
With all that out of the way, I'm gonna stick some of the dev-heavy things like passability issues and oddities in another spoiler.

The floating dots next to choices is very pretty, but maybe shrink their range a touch so they fly out about half the distance since from a quick glance it's hard to judge exactly which option they're next to

Battle issues:

Overall, this is a neat idea and pretty to look at, but it needs more tweaking and balancing to help keep players engaged. I'm looking forward to playing more in the future, once battles are polished a bit more.
Good luck with your project!

Gameplay
My #1 issue is the walk speed. I'm honestly curious as to why that decision was made. IMO, there's no reason to limit the player's movement that much in a game like this. It made exploration and progression a chore, and was one of the reasons I quit.
The combat system has a great concept. I like the idea of keeping an enemy alive to sap their ConP. The issue was that every enemy encounter played out the same way. Poise for a turn or two to get enough ConP to use the wind skill. Hope and pray it applies the state. Wait for your ConP to recharge. Use the wind skill...etc etc.

your
ConP, or is only vulnerable to lightning damage.

Also, since you don't really get anything from beating enemies aside from some notes, progression doesn't speed up like they normally do in RPG's.
Also, on that note (see what I did there?), I fought a ton of enemies and was only able to afford one ring (the ConP restoring one). I even started opening all the presents after I got the first upgrade from the fish statue.
The dungeon I played was fine. I don't like puzzles, but they weren't horrible.
I ended up getting the tools and than...I don't know. There was so much stuff to keep track of, I couldn't figure out where I needed to go next. Found a gate, but it needed a key that I didn't have.
I feel a similar way about some Zelda dungeons, but at least those have maps that make it a bit easier to navigate.
In the end, being lost in the dungeon, moving super slowly, having to fight every enemy in my way...I just lost interest. I made my way back to the town and decided to wander into the forest for kicks, but I quit after trying to reach a resource in the dark red puddle that make you walk even slower.
Bugs/Polish
Encountered a few bugs.
-The game in general does not run super well. The menu specifically takes a bit to load. Could be my computer, because I have a pretty lousy CPU.
-Not sure if this was intentional, but there was a random chicken sprite in some rooms?
-The battle you mentioned would crash, did not actually crash. Better get that fixed
-If you try to throw the fish into the lava before the tutorial, it doesn't work.
-Lots of items can be used in the menu that should not be (Ie, the rope)
-During one of the puzzles, when you can look around, you can get stuck in wall.
-Changing the BGM volume just won't work sometimes.
Anywho, I think with some work and changes this could be a really good game. Or maybe it's just not for me. Either way, good luck! It's great to see that you have a very solid chunk of the game done.

Pros
+
I do like the new photosensitivity/brightness warning at the start of the game.
+
So just gotta say right now - love, love, love the new sprite of Fidel. She (and Joy) are extremely adorable, and she has an incredible amount of personality with the way June depicts her.

The way Fidel mispronounces things is super cute, and it genuinely feels like she is in fact A Child and not what an adult thinks a child should act like.

This CG work at the beginning is pretty gorgeous. It feels art-game-y in a good way.

Music is consistently amazing. The battle theme in particular I can never get sick of.

HP Bars always being visible without having to mess with the default settings is very nice. It relieved a lot of the stress, if I had to be completely honest. (That said, the way they're all displayed regardless of whether you're selecting the enemy in question is pretty messy.)

I do think it's bizarre that you have soooo much custom SFX and art... yet you still use the base RTP sound effects for taking damage, healing and even use the bodyslam attack with the same SFX that I've seen in a million other games. You should really change this, since it's the sound effects we hear the most in combat!
-
Small nitpick, but in the tutorial where you have like, 20 icons to display the effects of juggling? It feels quite excessive, since it's literally just Wind -> Electric -> Fire repeated over and over. You could get away with just showing just the three and then (
and back again
), since a person's eyes can glaze over and think that the sequence changes somehow given how long you've made it.
-
I notice Fidel's sprite occasionally pop out of existence every now and then.
-
I hate unwinnable(?) battles like with the Maker Demon guy, especially after how Fidel gets a literal Super Saiyan power-up and unlocks all of her moves to fight him. Like you built it up like it's supposed to be a hype moment, yet it doesn't really matter.
-
Those are some very incomplete-looking menus.
-
I got legitimately softlocked after defeating the mimic! Fidel's sprite was fixed into her "item get" pose and I couldn't move, yet I could still open the menus and even save.
-
Was there supposed to be a penalty for letting the monster reach the top of the map first in that one sea dungeon cave?
-
Oops, I can see the edge of the world if I go to the far east in the sea dungeon map with the boat.
-
I had no idea what to do for that one puzzle where you had to light up all of the crystals before they ran out(?). Like am I missing something here? Was it meant to be a timing thing or a "correct order" thing?
-
So. I'm going to keep it real here. The fact Fidel cannot outrun enemies that chase her when they see her, especially since the only method of slowing them down is an object you gain after some way into a dungeon, is actively detrimental to the game's pace.
She moves at a permanent 4 speed while the enemies charge in at 5 speed, and keep in mind - your only method of stunning them has limited charges, and gaining new charges hurts Fidel! Every moment when I was able to successfully sneak past them felt like a miracle, since I did not want to deal with them.
THE BIG THING
:
-
I appreciate the attempt at making a game with low numbers. But despite this, the HP of the enemies is
Too Damn High
: combine this with the fact you always face like three-four dudes in one troop (maybe even more) and the fact
YOU CANNOT ESCAPE NO MATTER WHAT
... it felt extremely punishing in a way that made me question why I should even bother fighting enemies to begin with.
I understand the point of giving enemies high HP for something like this - you want to encourage the element-stacking system so the player will experiment and cycle between their skills when needed. Only issue is that by artificially bloating EVERY enemy's HP like this, especially if they're random encounters you're meant to deal with quickly, and throwing so many of them at the player...
It was stressful trying to avoid enemies on the map because of this, especially with the above issues with map movement. It felt like every single fight was a mini-boss encounter where you had to put in all of your effort, and demanding that same energy from every fight legitimately exhausted me.
-
Likewise, rewards were unbearably scarce compared to the effort it takes you just to defeat one troop / explore. If you could dispatch the enemies quickly, then it wouldn't be as much of an issue. (Seriously though, there was that fight that had four enemies but they only give you 3 rank points [your stand-in for EXP?])
I would think it'd be a great incentive if the first level/rank/thing was easily gained yet the subsequent levels would ask for more and more, or if it functioned like Paper Mario where you only need 100 to get a full level every time, but you get less star points from enemies you've already defeated over and over to dissuade the player from staying in the same spot over and over.
But as it stands, it's a bit of a slap to the face for so much effort, yeah?
-
The fact the element stack states
are NOT guaranteed
. There were multiple times in my playthrough that I tried to get combos going, but they just... refused to land on enemies. Blustery Day to set up an MP leech effect? Nope. Faraday Surge to paralyze an enemy? Nope. Not even Butane Lighter to set up damage over time. If you're going to revolve your game around this mechanic, at least make the effects always land!
This is also ignoring my issues with what it does to enemy design, since it boils down every enemy, regardless of their design or where you fight them in the game, to the identical blobs of stats that you dispatch in more or less the same way every time.
-
I should stress this right now in big bold print:
THE COMBAT WAS NOT HARD
.
I only died twice - first against the Maker and second against the fishman guy. Otherwise, I was able to keep myself afloat with Fidel's healing move every other time. But it should be stated that the
COMBAT WAS TOO
SLOW
. It also did not inspire confidence with the elemental system, since at one point I was like "Oh, this is going to be how the entire game plays, huh?" and that dampened my mood too.
-
The maps are too large for this walking speed. I'm aware you've been resistant to increasing the speed due to how it looks + have some kind of dashing upgrade in mind in the future based on a puzzle I came across at, but Fidel's walking speed combined with how huge the maps are make exploration a slog. Traversing the huge sea in particular felt like you could shrink the map down and/or position the islands closer to each other and you wouldn't lose much.
-
Fidel interacting with the librarian guy was my least favorite NPC interaction because it's just kind of annoying. It's the same joke of "young child argues with deaf old crackpot" for about 4 minutes, and I just kinda groaned when I knew where it was going.
A lot of conversations tend to drag on, now that I notice.
-
The Rat Gauntlet during the torch quest was too much for me, since I had already found the combat to be slow and uninteresting + my stamina had already been pushed due to all of the various stumbling blocks I experienced off-camera. I am not ashamed to say that, in my state of exhaustion, I quit playing since it felt like the straw that broke the camel's back.
?
I'm legitimately not sure how to feel about the dialogue between the Maker and the Pauper. Or any of the meta stuff beyond my positive initial reactions. Like is this a constructed world? Are Fidel or the rest of the inhabitants of the village not real people? If that's the case, then it'd make connecting to the people feel pretty worthless!
So I'm gonna echo what
@hiddenone
said: if you want the meta elements, either play into them more or just remove them entirely. Like Fidel is different because she's a real person or something?
Spoiler:
Overall Thoughts
The game has strong art direction - it's obvious from June's sprites and all of the cool effects (music, the echoing FX inside the void, the shop interface, maps, etc.) that you want this game to stand out compared to the crowd. Fidel, the title character, is also an adorable character that I'll never get tired of.
Unfortunately, the game stumbles due to a consistent huge issue -
speed
.
Combat is simultaneously not hard yet too slow - too many enemies with too much HP, doubled by the fact you cannot run from encounters once you get into them. Yet they run faster than you on the overworld if you can't use your limited use stunning function that only works from a certain distance. That also hurts you when you use it.
It made me question why there were on-screen encounters if you can't really dodge them, to quote a certain person here. Also, I'm glad to know Fidel's slow walking speed wasn't just a "me" issue, especially given how large the maps were.
That and the element juggling system doesn't really address that it suffers from the same thing most RPGs suffer from - poor encounter design. Because you can deal with all the enemies in the same way, more or less. The base system is interesting, but it stops at step 1, essentially.
That said, a lot of this is easily fixable. Trim down those HP counts, let the player escape combat, shrink the maps, make Fidel move faster, make the enemies drop more rewards. Oh, and make her start out with enough ConP to at least use one move before she has to Poise over and over to get new ones.

I feel this is a key disconnect with the combat. Fidel is this cute little child but she's continually getting into battles to the death with everything. I think player expectation with such a character is that combat would be light and easy.

feel

What can I say that hasn't already been said?
Spoiler:
Slaughty's Review
Well for starters...
During the intro boss battle, it crashed, I reloaded and then I never received the fire skill and I didn't know any better so I slogged through 3 hours of the slowest combat imaginable cursing Mr. Nolan for telling me to use WIND-LIGHTING-FIRE and not giving me the tools to do that. I came here to write a pretty scathing review when I read Alice's comment about burning everything and thought, "well.. maybe I hit a bug?" I restarted, it worked correctly and I walloped the Maker. Battles are way more fun being able to "juggle" compared to just wind-lighting over and over.
I decided to go to the Sea and played all the way through the boss, which somehow wasn't as bad as the 4 enemy troops I kept fighting. Battle theme is still stuck in my head as I write this. Only time I ever died was during my second playthrough, which is funny considering I actually had the necessary skills to win on my second playthrough, but by this point I wasn't paying as much attention to battles anymore and was just kind of done.
Sound & Music
are exceptional. This is where FatPP really shines! Headphones are a must, especially with the long reverb/echo on the sound effects. There's little flourishes during dialogue that really give the game whimsy. Audio fades in when you get close to the river. Music is really well done and fits the moods and theme of the game really well. I saved in town and left the game on the save screen and took a 10-minute break and came back to no music playing. It was kind of weird. Talked to the Beinon (I can't remember how it's spelled) and it started playing again. One critique, with all the custom sounds and music, there's still some animations that are stock with stock sounds, like when Fidel is getting attacked by an enemy in battle, but it's early, I'm sure you going to replace it.
Art & Aesthetics
are also really well done. The few custom sprites look amazing and have a certain charm to them. The character art and busts are phenomenal and Fidel and Joy's character designs are really cute and adorable. I like how Fidel has an idle animation, I'm just unsure how to feel about it. Maybe it's just me, but it looks like she's dancing. Like, oh no, monsters! Better break dance! or You sad? Better breakdance in the library! I love the Void area at the beginning, it really stands out and is unique. All the mapping is well done, standouts really go to the interior maps. The whole art direction of the game is very pleasant and uniform. It has a modern/modernish/clean feel to it.
What I didn't like was the font. It can be a little difficult to read at times with it's thin weight on a bright surface. Also the letter "e" will make a little line in the text box. The letter "e" & "c" look like twins, and the "f" & "t" can have their line faded out. I'm also not a fan of leaving Fidel's bust on screen when others are talking when they don't have a bust. It works well with Joy and that emo boy since they have busts but it can be a little confusing at times who is talking. Something else I noticed was I would read a text box, push confirm for the next one, and while my eyes are still at the bottom of the screen where the text box was, some action or a emote balloon would pop up and I would miss it as my eyes went from the bottom to the center of the screen. Maybe put a short pause or something.
Gameplay
is not bad, but it's not great either. The battle system needs more time in the oven. Maybe not so much frontloading at the beginning. I know it's hard to explain so I don't have any tips for this but as a player it's information overload since I just booted the game up.  It's not a bad idea, pretty unique, but very prescriptive in how it plays and buddy, every single battle plays out the same way. Poise (Guard) - leech - Poise again etc... There's little room for experimenting or playing in a different style than what is prescribed. Fighting 1 v 4 means 80% of actions are me standing around getting hit or waiting my turn. Battles are long and slow and there doesn't seem to be any actual variety to enemies besides how they look. Maybe I'm wrong, but they all "FEEL" the same. Possible recommendations would include reducing the number of enemies per troop, reducing enemy HP, having Fidel start off with some ConP or have it carry over from previous fights. Maybe have certain enemies start out with a stack or be immune/resistant to a stack or something. I used attack like 2 or three times and the game basically teaches you that it's worthless and you're better off guarding and then using a skill.
The town mechanics feel a little under explained. I like the idea of cleaning up the town or giving people gifts, but for what and more importantly WHY? Fidel says she wants everyone to be happy, but as a player I'm left wondering why because I don't know these people or care. I guess we just do it because it told us too and the rewards for doing this seem vague.
I really really like the Zelda style exploration and the on map tools, the warps back to town are a great QoL. I like how the map kind of goes back in on itself with shortcuts. The riddle/puzzle on the little islands was nice. Not complicated or requires knowledge outside of the game world (It's harder than people think). I got the lightning thing and while it's nice to be able to zap obstacles, the penalty being HP in a resource stingy game, seems counterintuitive to exploration. In fact there's a few design choices that almost make it seem like you didn't want us to explore. The slow walking speed with no dash option. I get that you wanted to slow the pacing down so it doesn't feel like a caffeinated toddler speeding around the map and make it more methodical & strategic but it turns exploration into a chore rather than an adventure. It suffers from the prescriptive element as the battle system, play it this way and only this way. Which is kind of weird when you have so many options in the options menu to customize gameplay and you also turn the player loose in town, go and do whatever you want.
Story & Writing
What little we can gleam of the story is pretty intriguing. The opening Void scene is the most captivating and really leaves the player with some questions. The dialogue is very well written, all the characters have their own voice, mannerisms, goals, and personalities. None of the jokes made me laugh out loud, but a few made chuckle. The back and forth with the librarian over stayed it's welcome and beat the joke into the ground. It was gold, and then it kept going, and going... For me, this was the case for a lot of the dialogue. It was competently well written, it just had a tendency to overstay its welcome. Joy and Fidel's meeting is really well done but at the same time just over stayed it's welcome for me. If you take a shot everytime a character just says" Yeah." you're going to need an ambulance. Fidel's mispronouncation is cute and gives her personality, although it can a little hard to read outload. The Meta elements are actually done really well and add more intrigue, but I have to agree with Hiddenone, that you're going to have to lean into more or remove it.
All the towns people seem fairly rounded out but what's Fidel's motivation besides, "make everyone in town happy."? Why? What difference does it make it? Why does Fidel care besides a childish view of the world? Why do I care as a player? After the intro my goal as a player is... Just wonder around and do what you want. Does Fidel want to get back home? Take revenge on the maker? Stop the Maker from doing something? Just live peacefully in the commune after making everyone happy?
Pacing
it's slow, you know that, I won't beat a dead horse into the ground. The combat is slow, the movement and exploration are slow and sometimes the dialogue is slow (either because it just keeps going or it interrupted something I was doing). I wonder if a stamina based dash would work at least for the dungeons or something.
Technical & Issues
This is weird because so much of the game is competently put together and you're doing a lot outside of typical RPG maker games but there's some weird things happening sometimes.
-There's a few passiblity errors: there's a few tiles in a house that are just floor but cannot be walked on. There's books on tables that appear over the character. etc.
-Opening the menu or coming out of certain houses in town would make the screen flicker and fade in an odd way.
-Saving, I get that you are doing a custom system but until that point I don't see why this is necessary. Just do Yanfly's for now like you are doing or do the default and just disallow saving in certain areas.
-There's a path in the sea area that goes down that doesn't have a fade in command and you are left playing blind trying to hit the transfer event back.
-Only happened once, leaving the cave with the fish statue in town didn't do the fade in command so I think I went back into the cave and back out but then I was standing on a hill that should've been impassible.
-I got the crash at the tutorial boss fight and then on subsequent game never received the fire skill.
-Keybinding is almost unusable to anyone outside of RPG maker. I can't read whatever is displayed over the keys and I know it's the Yanfly one but it has always felt unintuitive to me. Guess what, I also play with a controller so not being able to reload the lightning on the controller becuae there's no R key sucks.
-Would like some kind of HUD for the town stuff.
(Edited to add)
-interior maps: camera/screen scrolling would focus on the wrong area if the player goes back and forth repeatedly in the area where the camera pans over. I just wanted to see if I could break it, turn out you can.
Summary
It's still in early development so I get a lot of it is placeholder or will change. The art is amazing, the characters are fleshed out, it's a fairly unique concept and was never really UNFUN or anything like that. The Meta elements are really cool, the effects are awesome. The sound and music are really top notch above the rest. What really is eating you up is the pacing. I would just bring that up a little more. Not a lot, but it definitely crawls at times. I'm very interested to see where this projects goes as it shows a ton of potential and has a lot of love poured into it.
